entries.topicDescription: Networking layer patterns for production Android apps.

tips.title: Restrict retry-with-backoff to idempotent requests only
tips.content:
Automatically retrying a failed POST can duplicate side effects (double charges,
duplicate resource creation). Only GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are safe to retry
blindly under standard HTTP semantics — POST is idempotent only if your backend
explicitly guarantees it (e.g. via an idempotency key).

Gate your retry interceptor on the HTTP method, and use exponential backoff with
jitter rather than fixed delays to avoid thundering-herd retries across many
clients after an outage.

tips.title: Create one HttpClient and reuse it
tips.content:
An HttpClient owns a connection pool and background resources. Creating a new one for every request throws that away, wastes memory, and leaks resources if you forget to close it. Create a single client for the app (a singleton from your DI container), configure it once, and call close() only when the app is done with it.

Sharing one client also means one place to install plugins such as logging, timeouts and authentication.

tips.title: Set timeouts explicitly with the HttpTimeout plugin
tips.content:
Without the HttpTimeout plugin, a stalled request can wait far longer than a user will. Install it and set the three timeouts deliberately: how long a whole request may take, how long to wait to establish a connection, and how long the connection may stay silent between packets.

Set sensible defaults on the client and override them per request for the few calls that legitimately take longer, such as file uploads.

tips.title: Refresh bearer tokens with the Auth plugin
tips.content:
The Auth plugin's bearer provider attaches the access token to requests and, when the server answers 401, calls your refreshTokens block once and retries the request with the new tokens. You supply loadTokens (how to read stored tokens) and refreshTokens (how to obtain new ones).

Send the refresh call through a separate client without the Auth plugin, so a failed refresh can't trigger another refresh in a loop, and store the new tokens where loadTokens will read them.

tips.title: Ktor picks its engine per platform in Kotlin Multiplatform
tips.content:
Ktor separates the client API from the engine that does the networking. In a multiplatform project use the engine built for each platform: OkHttp on Android, Darwin (URLSession) on iOS. If you call HttpClient() without naming an engine, Ktor picks one that is on the classpath, so make sure each target's source set depends on exactly the engine you want.

Declare the client in common code and let each platform contribute its engine dependency.
